strengths: Identifies a concrete theoretical bottleneck in recent Clifford-Steerable CNNs (Zhdanov et al., 2024)—the basis incompleteness for vector-vector interactions—and provides an elegant solution by conditioning the implicit kernel network on equivariant input-derived multivectors.

The mathematical framework is sound and well-developed: the paper formally derives the steerability constraints for conditional convolutions (Lemma 4.2, 4.3, Proposition 4.5) and demonstrates via Clifford algebra product interactions how missing angular frequencies are recovered.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning four distinct PDE benchmarks across both Euclidean and pseudo-Euclidean domains (2D Navier-Stokes, 2D Shallow-Water, 3D Maxwell, and 2D+1 relativistic Maxwell).

Consistently delivers substantial performance gains over standard CSCNNs (30% to 55% error reduction) and remains competitive with or superior to state-of-the-art neural PDE solvers (e.g., Transolver, CViT).
Computational overhead is negligible: masked mean pooling adds less than 1% latency compared to standard CSCNNs while preserving translation-equivariance via template matching.
weaknesses: General completeness across arbitrary pseudo-orthogonal groups O(p, q) is posed only as a conjecture (Conjecture 4.7); the formal algebraic proof is provided and verified via symbolic algebra only for O(2, 0).
Results in Tables 1, 2, and 4 do not report error bars or standard deviations across multiple independent random runs / seeds to confirm statistical significance.

The conditioning operator investigated in the main experiments is restricted to global masked mean pooling; while practical and fast, exploration of more expressive, semi-local, or hierarchical conditioning operators remains preliminary.

strengths: Identifies and addresses a clear theoretical deficiency in prior Clifford-Steerable CNNs (CSCNNs), where the single-vector implicit kernel basis is over-constrained and missing frequency-2 components for vector-vector interactions under O(2).

Presents a mathematically rigorous formulation for conditional steerable convolutions (Definition 4.1, Lemma 4.2, Proposition 4.5), proving that conditioning on an equivariant summary operator T preserves full E(p, q) equivariance.

The practical realization via spatial masked mean pooling cleverly retains standard translation-equivariant template-matching convolution, introducing negligible computational overhead (<1% slowdown over CSCNN at inference).

Thorough empirical evaluation across four diverse PDE benchmarks (Navier-Stokes, Shallow-Water, 3D Maxwell, and 2+1D Relativistic Maxwell) demonstrating substantial error reductions (30% to 54%) compared to baseline CSCNNs and competitive performance against modern neural PDE solvers like Transolver and CViT.

Includes useful validation experiments, such as numerical verification of equivariance error (~10^-7), inference latency measurements, and ablation comparing equivariant pooling to non-equivariant random conditioning.
weaknesses: The claim of basis completeness in general pseudo-Euclidean spaces O(p, q) is formulated only as a conjecture (Conjecture 4.7); theoretical justification is restricted to algebraic symbolic calculations for O(2, 0).

While the theoretical framework admits general point-dependent conditioning K(x-y, f(x), f(y)), the actual implementation relies strictly on a single global mean-pooled vector per field, which acts as a global modulator rather than a truly spatially localized conditional kernel.

Quantitative results in Tables 1, 2, and 4 lack error bars or variance across multiple random seeds, which makes it harder to assess statistical significance in tightly contested comparisons (e.g., against Transolver).

strengths: Principled problem formulation: The paper clearly identifies and formalizes a critical limitation of standard Clifford-Steerable CNNs (CSCNNs), namely the incompleteness of the implicit kernel basis (e.g., missing frequency-2 angular components in O(2) vector-vector interactions due to geometric products on single vector inputs).

Sound theoretical framework: The mathematical extension from standard steerable convolution to conditional steerable convolution (Lemmas 4.2, 4.3, and Proposition 4.5) is cleanly formulated, maintaining exact E(p, q)-equivariance under an equivariant conditioning operator.

Computational efficiency: By utilizing an equivariant global summary operator (e.g., circular-masked spatial mean pooling), the approach preserves translation-invariant template matching during convolution, adding negligible computational and runtime overhead (~0.87% relative to unconditioned CSCNNs).

Comprehensive empirical validation: The method is evaluated across diverse PDE systems—including 2D fluid dynamics (Navier-Stokes, Shallow Water), 3D Maxwell, and 2+1D relativistic electrodynamics on pseudo-Euclidean space R^{1,2}—demonstrating consistent error reductions over standard CSCNNs (often >30-50% MSE reduction) and competitive performance against modern neural PDE baselines like Transolver.
weaknesses: Unproven general completeness: While the mechanism is demonstrated for O(2, 0) via symbolic analysis (Appendix A.4/A.5), Conjecture 4.7 regarding general completeness across arbitrary O(p, q) is unproven and left open.

Ambiguity regarding the source of empirical improvement: In the conditioning ablation (Table 3), conditioning on a fixed random multivector achieves an MSE of 0.3225 (compared to 0.2982 for mean pooling and 0.5699 for no conditioning). This indicates that a large fraction of the gain stems simply from introducing any secondary multivector to break the algebraic rank limitation of the geometric product on single vectors, rather than from dynamic input-dependent conditioning.

Degenerate input configurations: If the input feature field has zero (or near-zero) spatial mean (e.g., zero-mean divergence-free velocity fields or symmetric opposing vortices), T[f] vanishes, collapsing the conditional kernel back to the standard incomplete CSCNN kernel. The paper does not analyze or address this edge case.

Lack of statistical error bars: Tables 1, 2, and 4 report single-point MSE/relative L2 metrics without standard deviations or multi-seed evaluation, which is important for validating differences across closely performing baselines (e.g., Transolver vs. C-CSCNN).

Minor proof and typographical errors: In Appendix A.3, Equation (37) erroneously writes the identity K^(gz, ho(g)T[f]) = K^(gz, ho(g)T[f]) instead of equating the left-hand sides of Equations (35) and (36); on page 14 (Appendix C), there is a typo ('The dataset os obtained').

strengths: Identifies a clear and fundamental limitation in existing Clifford-Steerable CNNs (CSCNNs): the incompleteness of the implicit steerable kernel basis due to the inability of single-vector geometric products to propagate higher angular frequencies.

Provides a mathematically sound formulation of conditional steerable convolutions, rigorously deriving the steerability constraints under general group actions and proving equivariance when conditioned on invariant/equivariant global representations.

Offers a computationally practical design: utilizing a translation-invariant global pooling operator with circular masking preserves exact E(p,q) equivariance while retaining standard convolutional template matching efficiency.

Comprehensive empirical validation across diverse Euclidean and pseudo-Euclidean physical systems (2D Navier-Stokes, 2D Shallow Water, 3D Maxwell, and 2+1D Relativistic Maxwell), demonstrating consistent and significant gains over standard CSCNNs and competitive performance against state-of-the-art neural PDE solvers.
weaknesses: Overclaiming regarding completeness: The paper's title asserts a 'Complete Kernel Basis', but Section 4.4 states this property only as a conjecture (Conjecture 4.1). While the algebraic verification via SymPy in Appendix A.4–A.5 supports the recovery of frequency-2 terms in 2D O(2), a formal proof of completeness for general pseudo-orthogonal groups O(p, q) is absent.

Conceptual conflation of static kernel completeness versus dynamic/adaptive filtering: Conditioning kernels on global pooled features transforms the linear convolution into an input-dependent (non-linear/adaptive) operator. The empirical gains may stem partially from non-local context conditioning rather than purely 'completing' the underlying local linear kernel basis.

Lack of ablation studies: The paper only evaluates global mean pooling with circular masking. Ablations exploring alternative equivariant pooling methods (e.g., learned attention, higher-order moments), the impact of the circular mask, or comparing against unconditioned CSCNNs with increased layer depth/width would strengthen the analysis.

Presentation and experimental reporting issues: Experimental results in Figures 2 and 3 and Table 1 lack error bars or standard deviations across multiple random seeds. Additionally, there are minor referencing errors in Appendix D (referring to 'Table 6' which is formatted as Figure 6).

strengths: Addresses an important and recognized limitation of Clifford-Steerable CNNs (CSCNNs), namely the missing degrees of freedom (such as frequency-2 components in O(2) vector-vector interactions) in single-layer implicit steerable kernels.

The theoretical framing of conditional steerable convolutions (Definition 4.1, Lemma 4.1) and the reduction to an efficient template-matching convolution via a global equivariant operator T (Proposition 4.1) is mathematically principled and preserves exact continuous equivariance.

Strong and consistent empirical improvements across diverse physical PDE benchmarks (2D Navier-Stokes, 2D Shallow Water, 3D Maxwell, and 2+1D relativistic spacetime Maxwell) against relevant baselines including CSCNNs, Clifford ResNet, FNO, G-FNO, and Transolver.
Empirical verification of continuous group equivariance errors (Table 2), demonstrating that numerical equivariance is preserved to near machine precision.
weaknesses: Overclaiming on kernel completeness: The title and abstract assert a 'Complete Kernel Basis', but Section 4.4 explicitly downgrades this to an unproven conjecture (Conjecture 4.1: 'We therefore leave the proof for future work'). The only support provided is a symbolic SymPy calculation in 2D (Appendices A.4 and A.5), which does not constitute a proof of completeness for general O(p, q) or even general O(2).

Failure mode with symmetric or zero-mean fields: The practical implementation relies on global masked mean pooling T to extract the auxiliary multivector. If the input field has zero spatial mean (e.g., symmetric vortex pairs, zero-mean turbulence, divergence-free fields with zero net flux, or centered oscillatory fields), the conditioning multivector vanishes (zeta = 0). Under this condition, the kernel reduces identically to the original unconditioned CSCNN kernel and remains provably incomplete.

Input-dependent non-linear convolution vs. true steerable kernel: Conditioning the convolutional kernel on the input field f transforms the operator into an input-dependent, non-linear operator (similar to dynamic convolutions or continuous self-attention). Framing the resolution of linear steerable kernel basis incompleteness primarily through input-dependent non-linear conditioning is somewhat conceptually conflated.

Lack of statistical significance / error bars: Figures 2 and 3 report single mean performance curves across dataset sizes without standard deviations, confidence intervals, or indications of the number of random seeds used, which is critical in evaluating neural PDE solvers.

Presentation and typographical issues: There are formatting discrepancies and typos in the mathematical exposition, including undefined notation swaps in Appendix A.1 (switching from \rho_{in}, \rho_{out} to \rho_i, \rho_o in Eq. 24), an unclosed parenthesis in Eq. 34, and ambiguous colorbar labels in Figure 7.

strengths: Targeted motivation: The work directly addresses an established theoretical bottleneck of Clifford-Steerable CNNs (Zhdanov et al., 2024), namely the missing angular frequencies (such as frequency-2 vector-vector interactions) due to single-vector inputs to the geometric product.

Sound and practical design: Conditioning the implicit kernel network on a globally pooled multivector $T[f]$ preserves standard convolution efficiency (template matching / FFT) while enabling the geometric product to generate higher-order angular harmonics.
Rigorous equivariance derivation: The authors clearly formalize conditional steerable convolutions and prove $E(p, q)$-equivariance under an $O(p, q)$-equivariant conditioning operator $T$.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Evaluated across four diverse PDE benchmarks (2D Navier-Stokes, 2D Shallow Water, 3D Maxwell, and 2+1D relativistic Maxwell), showing consistent accuracy gains over baseline CSCNNs and standard baselines.
weaknesses: Overstatement of completeness in the title and narrative: The paper is titled 'Conditional Clifford-Steerable CNNs with Complete Kernel Basis', yet completeness is only formulated as an unproven conjecture (Conjecture 4.1) and illustrated via SymPy snippets for $O(2)$. Proving completeness for general $O(p, q)$ is left for future work.

Conceptual conflation of linear basis completeness and non-linear dynamic filtering: The incompleteness of standard steerable CNNs pertains to linear equivariant maps $\operatorname{Hom}_G(W_{\text{in}}, W_{\text{out}})$. Introducing input-dependent conditioning makes the convolutional layer non-linear (an input-dependent dynamic convolution), so framing this as completing the linear steerable basis is technically imprecise.

Lack of uncertainty estimation: Across Figures 2 and 3 and Table 1, no standard deviations or error bars across multiple random seeds are reported, making it difficult to judge statistical significance.

Minor presentation and mathematical typos: In Eq. 33, both sides of the equality are identical ($A = A$), which appears to be a copy-paste error from comparing Eq. 31 and Eq. 32; in Eq. 34, a closing parenthesis is missing ($T[\rho(g)f$); and in Appendix D, the text references 'Table 6' while the display is labeled 'Figure 6'.
